title: حِكَايَةُ التَّاجِرِ وَأَوْلَادِهِ
titleEn: The Merchant and His Sons, continued
part: Night 39 · The Merchant and His Sons, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 320–327 (Night 39, continuing directly from nights-38), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm exactly as Macnaghten prints it. Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition's Middle Arabic forms and its occasional compositor's slips, is preserved unaltered; a few genuinely obscure or corrupt-looking forms are vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes rather than silently repaired. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 39 continues the tale of Ghānim ibn Ayyūb. Newly arrived in Baghdad, he trades successfully, goes to a merchant's funeral, and is shut out of the city gate at midnight; he takes refuge in a walled tomb and climbs a palm. Three black slaves arrive carrying a chest, and to pass the time each begins to tell the story of how he came to be what he is: Bukhayt's tale, then Kāfūr's, which breaks off as dawn overtakes Shahrazād. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.
advisory: This night contains a passage, skipped for now, in which the first slave's tale describes sexual acts involving children.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ التَّاسِعَةُ وَالثَّلَٰثُونَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-tāsiʿatu wa-al-thalāthūna
sentences.l: And-when came-to-be the-night, the-ninth and-the-thirty,
sentences.i: When the thirty-ninth night came,
sentences.n: As on earlier nights, the print writes الثلثون without the alif of ثلاثون; it is kept as printed, with a dagger alif marking the long ā.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ ذَلِكَ التَّاجِرَ خَلَّفَ لَهُمَا مَالًا جَزِيلًا
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna dhālika al-tājira khallafa lahumā mālan jazīlan
sentences.l: She-said: It-reached-me, O-you king, the-fortunate, that that merchant left for-the-two-of-them wealth abundant,
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that the merchant left the two of them great wealth,
sentences.n: The print runs السعيد and ان together as one word, السعيدان; it is kept so, and read as al-saʿīdu anna. “The two of them” are the merchant’s children, Ghānim and his sister Fitna, as told at the end of the last night.

sentences.t: وَمِنْ جُمْلَةِ ذَلِكَ مِائَةُ حِمْلٍ مِنَ الْخَزِّ وَالدِّيبَاجِ وَنَوَافِحِ الْمِسْكِ وَمَكْتُوبٌ عَلَى الْأَحْمَالِ هَذَا مِمَّا عُمِلَ بِرَسْمِ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: wa-min jumlati dhālika miʾatu ḥimlin min al-khazzi wa-al-dībāji wa-nawāfiḥi al-miski wa-maktūbun ʿalā al-aḥmāli hādhā mimmā ʿumila bi-rasmi baghdāda
sentences.l: And-from sum-of that, a-hundred load of the-silk and-the-brocade and-pods-of the-musk; and written upon the-loads: This (is) of-what was-made for-the-account-of Baghdad.
sentences.i: Among it were a hundred loads of silk and brocade and pods of musk, and on the loads was written, “This is of the goods made for Baghdad.”
sentences.n: نوافح المسك are musk-pods, the glands from which musk was taken. بِرَسْمِ means “destined for, in the name of”, as on a shipping mark. The print itself puts a damma on ع of عُمل, and it is kept.

sentences.t: وَكَانَتْ نِيَّتُهُ السَّفَرُ إِلَى بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: wa-kānat niyyatuhu al-safaru ilā baghdāda
sentences.l: And-was his-intention the-travel to Baghdad.
sentences.i: It had been his intention to travel to Baghdad.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا تَوَفَّاهُ اللَّهُ تَعَالَى وَمَضَتْ مُدَّةٌ أَخَذَ وَلَدُهُ هَذِهِ الْأَحْمَالَ وَسَافَرَ بِهَا إِلَى بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā tawaffāhu allāhu taʿālā wa-maḍat muddatun akhadha waladuhu hādhihi al-aḥmāla wa-sāfara bihā ilā baghdāda
sentences.l: And-when took-him-in-death God, exalted-is-He, and-passed a-while, took his-son these the-loads and-travelled with-them to Baghdad.
sentences.i: When God Most High had taken him, and some time had passed, his son took these loads and set out with them for Baghdad.
sentences.n: The main verb أخذ follows the lammā-clauses with no fa-; this is ordinary in narrative. The merchant’s son is Ghānim ibn Ayyūb.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ ذَلِكَ فِي زَمَنِ الْخَلِيفَةِ هَارُونَ الرَّشِيدِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna dhālika fī zamani al-khalīfati hārūna al-rashīdi
sentences.l: And-was that in time-of the-caliph Hārūn the-rightly-guided.
sentences.i: This was in the days of the caliph Hārūn al-Rashīd.

sentences.t: وَوَدَّعَ أُمَّهُ وَأَقَارِبَهُ وَأَهْلَ بَلْدَتِهِ قَبْلَ سَيْرِهِ وَخَرَجَ مُتَوَكِّلًا عَلَى اللَّهِ تَعَالَى وَكَتَبَ اللَّهُ لَهُ السَّلَامَةَ حَتَّى وَصَلَ إِلَى بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: wa-waddaʿa ummahu wa-aqāribahu wa-ahla baladatihi qabla sayrihi wa-kharaja mutawakkilan ʿalā allāhi taʿālā wa-kataba allāhu lahu al-salāmata ḥattā waṣala ilā baghdāda
sentences.l: And-he-bade-farewell-to his-mother and-his-relatives and-people-of his-town before his-going, and-went-out relying upon God, exalted-is-He, and-wrote God for-him the-safety until he-arrived at Baghdad.
sentences.i: He took leave of his mother, his kinsfolk and the people of his town before setting out, and went forth putting his trust in God Most High; and God decreed him safety until he reached Baghdad.
sentences.n: كتب الله له السلامة, literally “God wrote safety for him”, means God decreed it, as if in a ledger.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ صُحْبَتَهُ جَمَاعَةٌ مِنَ التُّجَّارِ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna ṣuḥbatahu jamāʿatun min al-tujjāri
sentences.l: And-was in-his-company a-group of the-merchants.
sentences.i: A band of merchants travelled in his company.
sentences.n: صحبته stands as an adverb (“in his company”), accusative, ahead of the subject جماعة, which is why kāna stays singular.

sentences.t: فَاكْتَرَى لَهُ دَارًا حَسَنَهْ وَفَرَشَهَا بِالْبُسُطِ وَالْوَسَائِدِ وَأَرْخَى عَلَيْهَا السُّتُورَ وَأَنْزَلَ فِيهَا تِلْكَ الْأَحْمَالَ وَالْبِغَالَ وَالْجِمَالَ وَجَلَسَ حَتَّى اسْتَرَاحَ وَسَلَّمَتْ عَلَيْهِ التُّجَّارُ وَأَكَابِرُ بَغْدَادَ
sentences.tr: fa-iktarā lahu dāran ḥasanah wa-farashahā bi-al-busuṭi wa-al-wasāʾidi wa-arkhā ʿalayhā al-sutūra wa-anzala fīhā tilka al-aḥmāla wa-al-bighāla wa-al-jimāla wa-jalasa ḥattā istarāḥa wa-sallamat ʿalayhi al-tujjāru wa-akābiru baghdāda
sentences.l: So-he-hired for-himself a-house fine, and-furnished-it with-the-carpets and-the-cushions, and-let-down over-it the-curtains, and-lodged in-it those the-loads and-the-mules and-the-camels; and-sat until he-rested, and-greeted upon-him the-merchants and-the-greatest-ones-of Baghdad.
sentences.i: He hired himself a handsome house, furnished it with carpets and cushions, and hung curtains in it; he lodged in it those loads, with the mules and the camels, and sat until he was rested. Then the merchants and the notables of Baghdad came and gave him greeting.
sentences.n: حسنه is printed with final hāʾ, not tāʾ marbūṭa, and is read in pause (ḥasanah): a Middle Arabic spelling, kept. سلمت is feminine singular before the plural التجار, which is regular for a plural subject that follows its verb.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ أَخَذَ بُقْجَةً فِيهَا عَشْرُ تَفَاصِيلَ مِنَ الْقُمَاشِ النَّفِيسِ مَكْتُوبٍ عَلَيْهَا ثَمَنُهَا وَنَزَلَ بِهَا إِلَى سُوقِ التُّجَّارِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu akhadha buqjatan fīhā ʿashru tafāṣīla min al-qumāshi al-nafīsi maktūbin ʿalayhā thamanuhā wa-nazala bihā ilā sūqi al-tujjāri
sentences.l: Then that-he took a-bundle, in-it ten cuts from the-cloth, the-precious, written upon-them their-price; and-went-down with-it to market-of the-merchants.
sentences.i: Then he took a bundle containing ten lengths of costly cloth, with their prices written on them, and went down with it to the merchants’ market.
sentences.n: بقجة is a bundle wrapped in cloth (Turkish bohça); a few lines on the same bundle is spelled بقشة. تفاصيل (plural of تفصيلة) are cuts or lengths of cloth, enough for a garment.

sentences.t: فَتَلَقَّوْهُ بِالتَّرْحِيبِ وَسَلَّمُوا عَلَيْهِ وَأَكْرَمُوهُ وَأَنْزَلُوهُ وَأَجْلَسُوهُ عَلَى دُكَّانِ شَيْخِ السُّوقِ
sentences.tr: fa-talaqqawhu bi-al-tarḥībi wa-sallamū ʿalayhi wa-akramūhu wa-anzalūhu wa-ajlasūhu ʿalā dukkāni shaykhi al-sūqi
sentences.l: So-they-met-him with-the-welcome, and-greeted upon-him, and-honoured-him, and-brought-him-down, and-seated-him upon the-bench-of elder-of the-market.
sentences.i: The merchants met him with a welcome, greeted him and did him honour; they helped him down and seated him on the bench of the shaykh of the market.
sentences.n: شيخ السوق is the head of the market’s merchants, the one who oversees its trade; دكان is a shop-bench or stall.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ نَاوَلَهُ الْبُقْشَةَ فَفَتَحَهَا وَأَخْرَجَ مِنْهَا تَفَاصِيلَ فَبَاعَ لَهُ شَيْخُ السُّوقِ التَّفَاصِيلَ فَرَبِحَ فِي كُلِّ دِينَارٍ دِينَارَيْنِ مِثْلَهُ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu nāwalahu al-buqshata fa-fataḥahā wa-akhraja minhā tafāṣīla fa-bāʿa lahu shaykhu al-sūqi al-tafāṣīla fa-rabiḥa fī kulli dīnārin dīnārayni mithlahu
sentences.l: Then that-he handed-him the-bundle, and-he-opened-it and-took-out from-it cuts; and-sold for-him the-elder-of the-market the-cuts, and-he-gained in every dinar two-dinars, the-like-of-it.
sentences.i: Then he handed him the bundle, and the shaykh opened it, took out some lengths and sold them for him; and Ghānim made a profit of two dinars on every dinar.
sentences.n: The last words, دينارين مثله, are puzzling: the dual with “the like of it” may be a slip for “a dinar like it”, a profit equal to the outlay. The text is kept as printed and read as a profit of two dinars on the dinar.

sentences.t: فَفَرِحَ غَانِمٌ وَصَارَ يَبِيعُ الْقُمَاشَ وَالتَّفَاصِيلَ أَوَّلًا بِأَوَّلٍ وَلَمْ يَزَلْ كَذَلِكَ إِلَى مُدَّةِ سَنَةٍ كَامِلَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-fariḥa ghānimun wa-ṣāra yabīʿu al-qumāsha wa-al-tafāṣīla awwalan bi-awwalin wa-lam yazal kadhālika ilā muddati sanatin kāmilatin
sentences.l: So-rejoiced Ghānim, and-became selling the-cloth and-the-cuts first by first; and-not he-ceased thus until period-of a-year complete.
sentences.i: Ghānim was delighted, and he went on selling his cloth and his lengths one lot after another, and so he continued for a full year.
sentences.n: أولا بأول (“first by first”) is a common idiom for “one after the other, as each came up”. ولم يزل كذلك is “and he did not cease being so”.

sentences.t: وَفِي أَوَّلِ السَّنَةِ الثَّانِيَةِ جَاءَ إِلَى الْقَيْصَرِيَّةِ الَّتِي فِى السُّوقِ فَرَأَى بَابَهَا مَغْلُوقًا فَسَأَلَ عَنْ سَبَبِ ذَلِكَ
sentences.tr: wa-fī awwali al-sanati al-thāniyati jāʾa ilā al-qaysariyyati allatī fī al-sūqi fa-raʾā bābahā maghlūqan fa-saʾala ʿan sababi dhālika
sentences.l: And-in beginning-of the-year the-second he-came to the-covered-market which in the-market, and-saw its-door closed, and-asked about cause-of that.
sentences.i: At the beginning of the second year he came to the covered market in the bazaar and saw its door shut, and he asked the reason.
sentences.n: القيصرية is a covered market-hall for fine goods. مغلوقا is the colloquial-leaning participle “shut” (Classical مُغْلَق). Here the print spells فى with a dotless ى, kept in the Arabic.

sentences.t: فَقِيلَ لَهُ إِنَّ وَاحِدًا مِنَ التُّجَّارِ تُوُفِّيَ وَذَهَبَ التُّجَّارُ كُلُّهُمْ يَمْشُونَ فِي جَنَازَتِهِ فَهَلْ لَكَ أَنْ تَكْسِبَ أَجْرًا وَتَمْشِيَ مَعَهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qīla lahu inna wāḥidan min al-tujjāri tuwuffiya wa-dhahaba al-tujjāru kulluhum yamshūna fī janāzatihi fa-hal laka an taksiba ajran wa-tamshiya maʿahum
sentences.l: So-it-was-said to-him: Indeed one from the-merchants was-taken-in-death, and-went the-merchants, all-of-them, walking in his-funeral; so is-there for-you that you-earn a-reward and-walk with-them?
sentences.i: He was told, “One of the merchants has died, and all the merchants have gone to walk in his funeral procession. Would you not like to earn a reward and walk with them?”
sentences.n: Walking behind a funeral and sharing in the burial earns a religious reward (أجر), which is why the question is put to a stranger.

sentences.t: قَالَ نَعَمْ
sentences.tr: qāla naʿam
sentences.l: He-said: Yes.
sentences.i: “Yes,” he said.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ سَأَلَ عَنْ مَحَلِّ الْجَنَازَةِ فَدَلُّوهُ عَلَى الْمَحَلِّ فَتَوَضَّأَ ثُمَّ مَشَى مَعَ التُّجَّارِ إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلُوا إِلَى الْمُصَلَّى
sentences.tr: thumma saʾala ʿan maḥalli al-janāzati fa-dallūhu ʿalā al-maḥalli fa-tawaḍḍaʾa thumma mashā maʿa al-tujjāri ilā an waṣalū ilā al-muṣallā
sentences.l: Then he-asked about place-of the-funeral, and-they-guided-him to the-place; and-he-performed-ablution, then walked with the-merchants until that they-arrived at the-place-of-prayer.
sentences.i: Then he asked where the funeral was, and they directed him to the place; he made his ablutions and walked with the merchants until they reached the prayer ground.
sentences.n: المصلى is the open ground or hall set aside for prayer, here for the funeral prayer. The print has a precomposed hamza in فتوضأ, so it is kept as printed.

sentences.t: وَصَلَّوْا عَلَى الْمَيِّتِ ثُمَّ مَشَى التُّجَّارُ جَمِيعُهُمْ قُدَّامَ الْجَنَازَةِ إِلَى الْمَقْبَرَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣallaw ʿalā al-mayyiti thumma mashā al-tujjāru jamīʿuhum quddāma al-janāzati ilā al-maqbarati
sentences.l: And-they-prayed upon the-dead, then walked the-merchants, all-of-them, in-front-of the-funeral to the-graveyard.
sentences.i: They prayed over the dead man, and then all the merchants walked in front of the bier to the graveyard.

sentences.t: فَتَبِعَهُمْ غَانِمٌ مِنْ حَيَاءٍ وَقَدْ خَرَجُوا بِالْجَنَازَةِ مِنْ بَغْدَادَ إِلَى خَارِجِ الْمَدِينَةِ وَشَقُّوا بَيْنَ الْمَقَابِرِ إِلَى أَنْ وَصَلُوا إِلَى الْمَدْفَنِ
sentences.tr: fa-tabiʿahum ghānimun min ḥayāʾin wa-qad kharajū bi-al-janāzati min baghdāda ilā khāriji al-madīnati wa-shaqqū bayna al-maqābiri ilā an waṣalū ilā al-madfani
sentences.l: So-followed-them Ghānim out-of shyness, and-already they-had-gone-out with-the-funeral from Baghdad to outside-of the-city, and-cleaved between the-graves until that they-arrived at the-burial-place.
sentences.i: Ghānim followed them out of bashfulness. By now they had carried the bier out of Baghdad to the outskirts of the city, and they threaded their way among the graves until they reached the burial place.
sentences.n: حياء is shyness or a sense of propriety: Ghānim goes on because he is too bashful to turn back. وقد خرجوا gives the background: they had already left the city.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدُوا أَهْلَ الْمَيِّتِ قَدْ نَصَبُوا الْخَيْمَةَ عَلَى الْقَبْرِ وَأَحْضَرُوا الشُّمُوعَ وَالْقَنَادِيلَ
sentences.tr: fa-wajadū ahla al-mayyiti qad naṣabū al-khayamata ʿalā al-qabri wa-aḥḍarū al-shumūʿa wa-al-qanādīla
sentences.l: So-they-found people-of the-dead, they-had pitched the-tent over the-grave and-brought-in the-candles and-the-lamps.
sentences.i: There they found the dead man’s family, who had pitched a tent over the grave and brought candles and lamps.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ دَفَنُوا الْمَيِّتَ وَجَلَسَ الْقُرَّاءُ يَقْرَءُونَ الْقُرْآنَ عَلَى ذَلِكَ الْقَبْرِ
sentences.tr: thumma dafanū al-mayyita wa-jalasa al-qurrāʾu yaqraʾūna al-qurʾāna ʿalā dhālika al-qabri
sentences.l: Then they-buried the-dead, and-sat the-reciters reading the-Recitation upon that the-grave.
sentences.i: Then they buried the dead man, and the reciters sat reading the Qurʾān at the grave.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسَ تِلْكَ التُّجَّارُ فَجَلَسَ مَعَهُمْ غَانِمُ بْنُ أَيُّوبَ وَهُوَ غَالِبٌ عَلَيْهِ الْحَيَاءُ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasa tilka al-tujjāru fa-jalasa maʿahum ghānimu ibnu ayyūba wa-huwa ghālibun ʿalayhi al-ḥayāʾu
sentences.l: So-sat those the-merchants, and-sat with-them Ghānim son-of Ayyūb, and-he, prevailing upon-him (was) the-shyness.
sentences.i: The merchants sat down, and Ghānim ibn Ayyūb sat down with them, overmastered by shyness.
sentences.n: تلك التجار is a Middle Arabic form: the feminine-singular demonstrative “that” with a plural of persons, where Classical would say أولئك. Kept as printed.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ أَنَا لَمْ أَقْدِرْ أَنْ أُفَارِقَهُمْ حَتَّى أَنْصَرِفَ مَعَهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla fī nafsihi anā lam aqdir an ufāriqahum ḥattā anṣarifa maʿahum
sentences.l: So-he-said in his-self: I, not I-was-able that I-part-from-them until I-depart with-them …
sentences.i: He said to himself, “I cannot leave them until I go back with them …”
sentences.n: The thought breaks off here and is finished in the next unit. لم أقدر (“I did not manage”) is meant as “I cannot”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ جَلَسُوا يَسْمَعُونَ الْقُرْآنَ إِلَى وَقْتِ الْعِشَاءِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahum jalasū yasmaʿūna al-qurʾāna ilā waqti al-ʿishāʾi
sentences.l: Then, indeed-they, they-sat, hearing the-recitation, to the-time of-the-evening.
sentences.i: Then they sat listening to the recitation of the Qurʾān until the hour of the evening meal.
sentences.n: Ghānim is now a guest at a gathering of merchants outside Baghdad, listening to the recitation of the Qurʾān. القرآن is printed with the precomposed آ, which is kept.

sentences.t: فَقَدَّمُوا لَهُمُ الْعِشَاءَ وَالْحَلْوَى فَأَكَلُوا حَتَّى اكْتَفَوْا وَغَسَلُوا أَيْدِيَهُمْ ثُمَّ جَلَسُوا مَكَانَهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qaddamū lahumu al-ʿishāʾa wa-al-ḥalwā fa-akalū ḥattā iktafaw wa-ghasalū aydiyahum thumma jalasū makānahum
sentences.l: So-they-presented to-them the-supper and-the-sweet, so-they-ate until they-were-satisfied, and-they-washed their-hands, then they-sat their-place.
sentences.i: So they set the supper and the sweetmeats before them, and they ate until they had their fill, and washed their hands, and then sat again in their places.

sentences.t: فَاشْتَغَلَ خَاطِرُ غَانِمٍ بِمَكَانِهِ وَبِضَاعَتِهِ وَخَافَ مِنَ اللُّصُوصِ
sentences.tr: fa-ishtaghala khāṭiru ghānimin bi-makānihi wa-biḍāʿatihi wa-khāfa mina al-luṣūṣi
sentences.l: So-became-occupied the-mind of-Ghānim with-his-place and-with-his-merchandise, and-he-feared from the-thieves.
sentences.i: But Ghānim’s mind was busy with the place where he had left his goods and his merchandise, and he grew afraid of thieves.
sentences.n: اشتغل خاطر X means “X’s mind was taken up (with worry)”; here the worry concerns the lodging where his wares lay, which he had left behind in the city.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ أَنَارَجُلٌ غَرِيبٌ وَمُتَّهَمٌ بِالْمَالِ فَإِنْ بِتُّ اللَّيْلَةَ بَعِيدًا عَنْ مَنْزِلِي يَسْرِقُ اللُّصُوصُ مَا فِيهِ مِنَ الْمَالِ وَالْأَحْمَالِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla fī nafsihi anā rajulun gharībun wa-muttahamun bi-al-māli fa-in bittu al-laylata baʿīdan ʿan manzilī yasriqu al-luṣūṣu mā fīhi mina al-māli wa-al-aḥmāli
sentences.l: So-he-said in his-self: I-man a-stranger, and-accused with-the-wealth; so-if I-spend-the-night the-night far from my-lodging, the-thieves steal what is-in-it of the-wealth and-the-loads.
sentences.i: And he said to himself, “I am a stranger here, and a man known to carry wealth. If I pass this night far from my lodging, thieves will steal everything in it, the money and the bales.”
sentences.n: أنارجل is printed as one word, أنا + رجل, and is kept so. The apodosis يسرق is indicative and has no fa-; Classical Arabic would want the jussive يسرقِ with فـ. متهم بالمال can also mean “suspected of having money”: a man thought to be rich.

sentences.t: وَخَافَ عَلَى مَتَاعِهِ فَقَامَ وَخَرَجَ مِنْ بَيْنِ الْجَمَاعَةِ وَاسْتَأْذَنَهُمْ عَلَى أَنَّهُ يَقْضِي حَاجَةً فَصَارَ يَمْشِي وَيَتْبَعُ آثَارَ الطَّرِيقِ حَتَّى جَاءَ إِلَى بَابِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: wa-khāfa ʿalā matāʿihi fa-qāma wa-kharaja min bayni al-jamāʿati wa-istaʾdhanahum ʿalā annahu yaqḍī ḥājatan fa-ṣāra yamshī wa-yatbaʿu āthāra al-ṭarīqi ḥattā jāʾa ilā bābi al-madīnati
sentences.l: And-he-feared for his-belongings, so-he-rose and-went-out from between the-company and-asked-their-leave on-that-he would-fulfil a-need; so-he-became walking and-following the-traces of-the-road until he-came to the-gate of-the-city.
sentences.i: He feared for his belongings, so he rose and went out from among the company, asking their leave on the pretext that he had a need to attend to. Then he walked on, following the traces of the road, until he came to the city gate.
sentences.n: يقضي حاجة, “to fulfil a need”, is the polite phrase for relieving oneself; it is the excuse Ghānim gives. صار يمشي (“he became walking”) is the Middle Arabic way of saying “he went on walking”.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ ذَٰلِكَ الْوَقْتُ نِصْفَ اللَّيْلِ فَوَجَدَ بَابَ الْمَدِينَةِ مَغْلُوقًا وَلَمْ يَرَ أَحَدٌ غَادِيًا وَلَا رَائِحًا وَ لَمْ يَسْمَعْ صَوْتًا سِوَى الْكِلَابِ يَنْبَحُونَ وَالذِّيَابِ يَصِيحُونَ فَرَجَعَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna dhālika al-waqtu niṣfa al-layli fa-wajada bāba al-madīnati maghlūqan wa-lam yara aḥadun ghādiyan wa-lā rāʾiḥan wa-lam yasmaʿ ṣawtan siwā al-kilābi yanbaḥūna wa-al-dhiyābi yaṣīḥūna fa-rajaʿa
sentences.l: And-was that the-time the-half of-the-night; so-he-found the-gate of-the-city locked, and-not saw anyone going-out-in-the-morning nor going-out-in-the-evening, and not he-heard a-sound other-than the-dogs barking and-the-wolves howling; so-he-returned.
sentences.i: It was then the middle of the night. He found the city gate locked, and he saw no one going out or coming in, and he heard no sound but the dogs barking and the wolves howling; so he turned back.
sentences.n: The print has a stray space in و لم (the و stands at the end of one printed line, لم at the start of the next); it is kept as printed. مغلوق for “locked” is the colloquial passive participle; Classical has مُغْلَق. الذياب, “wolves”, is the colloquial plural of ذِئْب, written without the hamza; Classical has ذِئَاب. غاديا ولا رائحا (“going out in the morning nor in the evening”) is a stock pair meaning “anyone coming or going”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَاحَوْلَ وَلَاقُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّٰهِ كُنْتُ خَائِفًا عَلَى مَالِي وَجِئْتُ لِأَ جْلِهِ فَوَجَدْتُ الْبَابَ مَغْلُوقًا وَبَقِيتُ الْآنَ خَائِفًا عَلَى رُوحِي
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lāḥawla wa-lāquwwata illā bi-allāhi kuntu khāʾifan ʿalā mālī wa-jiʾtu li-ajlihi fa-wajadtu al-bāba maghlūqan wa-baqītu al-āna khāʾifan ʿalā rūḥī
sentences.l: And-he-said: No-power and-no-strength except with-God! I-was fearing for my-wealth, and-I-came for its-sake, and-I-found the-gate locked, and-I-remained now fearing for my-soul.
sentences.i: And he said, “There is no power and no strength save in God! I was afraid for my wealth, and I came here for its sake, and I found the gate locked; and now I am left afraid for my very life.”
sentences.n: لاحول ولاقوة is printed with the لا joined to the following word; it is the common formula of dismay, “there is no power nor strength save through God”. لا جله is printed as two words, لأجله “for its sake”; the split is kept. روحي is “my soul”, here as in colloquial speech “my life”.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُ رَجَعَ وَرَاءَهُ يَنْظُرُ لَهُ مَحَلًّا يَنَامُ فِيهِ إِلَى الصَّبَاحِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahu rajaʿa warāʾahu yanẓuru lahu maḥallan yanāmu fīhi ilā al-ṣabāḥi
sentences.l: Then, indeed-he, he-returned behind-him, looking for-himself a-place he-sleeps in-it until the-morning.
sentences.i: Then he went back the way he had come, looking for a place where he might sleep until morning.
sentences.n: رجع وراءه, “he went back behind him”, is an idiom for turning back on one’s own track. ينظر له محلا: “looking out for himself a place”; the له is the so-called dative of interest.

sentences.t: فَوَجَدَ تُرْبَةً مُحَوَّطَةً بِأَرْبَعِ حِيطَانٍ وَفِيهَا نَخْلَةٌ وَلَهَا بَابٌ مِنَ الصَّوَّانِ مَفْتُوحٌ
sentences.tr: fa-wajada turbatan muḥawwaṭatan bi-arbaʿi ḥīṭānin wa-fīhā nakhlatun wa-lahā bābun mina al-ṣawwāni maftūḥun
sentences.l: So-he-found a-tomb-enclosure walled with-four walls, and-in-it a-palm, and-for-it a-door of the-flint open.
sentences.i: He came upon a burial enclosure, walled in with four walls, with a palm tree inside it and a door of flint standing open.
sentences.n: تربة is the walled tomb-enclosure, a family burial ground. The print itself puts shaddas on الصّوّان, and they are kept; the word means flint or hard stone. مفتوح follows the indefinite باب, so it can be read as a description of it, “a door … open”.

sentences.t: فَدَخَلَهَا وَأَرَادَ أَنْ يَنَامَ فِيهَا فَلَمْ يَجِئْهُ نَوْمٌ وَأَخَذَتْهُ رَجْفَةٌ وَوَحْشَةٌ وَهُوَ بَيْنَ الْقُبُورِ
sentences.tr: fa-dakhalahā wa-arāda an yanāma fīhā fa-lam yajiʾhu nawmun wa-akhadhathu rajfatun wa-waḥshatun wa-huwa bayna al-qubūri
sentences.l: So-he-entered-it and-wanted to he-sleep in-it, but-not came-to-him sleep, and-seized-him a-trembling and-a-desolation, while-he between the-graves.
sentences.i: He went in and meant to sleep there, but sleep would not come to him; a trembling and a dread came over him, for he was among the graves.
sentences.n: وحشة is the loneliness and unease of an empty, frightening place.

sentences.t: فَقَامَ وَاقِفًا عَلَى قَدَمَيْهِ وَفَتَحَ بَابَ الْمَكَانِ وَنَظَرَ فَإِذَا هُوَ بِنُورٍ عَلَى بُعْدٍ فِي نَاحِيَةِ بَابِ الْمَدِينَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāma wāqifan ʿalā qadamayhi wa-fataḥa bāba al-makāni wa-naẓara fa-idhā huwa bi-nūrin ʿalā buʿdin fī nāḥiyati bābi al-madīnati
sentences.l: So-he-rose standing on his-two-feet, and-opened the-door of-the-place and-looked, and-behold he with-a-light at a-distance in the-direction of-the-gate of-the-city.
sentences.i: He sprang up and stood on his feet, and opened the door of the place and looked out; and behold, there was a light in the distance, over toward the city gate.
sentences.n: In فإذا هو بنور the بـ only marks what appears: “and behold, a light”.

sentences.t: فَمَشَى قَلِيلًا فَرَأيٰ النُّورَ فِى الطَّرِيقِ الَّتِي تُؤَدِّي إِلَى التُّرْبَةِ الَّتِي هُوَ فِيهَا
sentences.tr: fa-mashā qalīlan fa-raʾā al-nūra fī al-ṭarīqi allatī tuʾaddī ilā al-turbati allatī huwa fīhā
sentences.l: So-he-walked a-little, and-saw the-light in the-road which leads to the-tomb-enclosure which he in-it.
sentences.i: He walked a little way and saw the light on the road that leads to the very enclosure where he stood.
sentences.n: راي is printed with a final ي; it is read رأى with a dagger alif over the ي, which keeps the printed spelling. Here the print writes تودي for تؤدّي without the hamza.

sentences.t: فَخَافَ غَانِمٌ عَلَى نَفْسِهِ وَأَسْرَعَ بِرَدِّ الْبَابِ وَتَعَلَّقَ حَتَّى طَلَعَ فَوْقَ النَّخْلَةِ وَتَدَارَى فِي قَلْبِهَا
sentences.tr: fa-khāfa ghānimun ʿalā nafsihi wa-asraʿa bi-radd al-bābi wa-taʿallaqa ḥattā ṭalaʿa fawqa al-nakhlati wa-tadārā fī qalbihā
sentences.l: So-feared Ghānim for his-self, and-hurried with-the-pushing-back of-the-door, and-clung until he-climbed above the-palm, and-hid in its-heart.
sentences.i: Ghānim grew afraid for his life, and made haste to shut the door, and clung and climbed to the top of the palm, and hid himself in its heart.
sentences.n: أسرع برد الباب: the verb takes بـ, “he hurried with (the act of) closing the door”. قلب النخلة is the leafy crown of the palm, its “heart”, where he could hide among the fronds.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ النُّورُ يَتَقَرَّبُ مِنَ التُّرْبَةِ شَيْئًا فَشَيْئًا حَتَّى قَرُبَ مِنَ التُّرْبَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra al-nūru yataqarrabu mina al-turbati shayʾan fa-shayʾan ḥattā qaruba mina al-turbati
sentences.l: So-became the-light drawing-near from the-tomb-enclosure little by-little until it-neared the-tomb-enclosure.
sentences.i: The light came closer to the enclosure, little by little, until it was close beside it.

sentences.t: فَتَأَمَّلَ النُّورَ فَرَأَى ثَلَٰثَةَ عَبِيدٍ اثْنَانِ شَائِلَانِ صُنْدُوقًا وَوَاحِدٌ فِي يَدِهِ فَانُوسٌ وَفَأْسٌ
sentences.tr: fa-taʾammala al-nūra fa-raʾā thalāthata ʿabīdin ithnāni shāʾilāni ṣundūqan wa-wāḥidun fī yadihi fānūsun wa-faʾsun
sentences.l: So-he-gazed at-the-light, and-saw three slaves: two carrying a-chest, and-one in his-hand a-lantern and-an-axe.
sentences.i: He gazed at the light and saw three black slaves: two of them carrying a chest, and one with a lantern and an axe in his hand.
sentences.n: ثلثة is printed without the alif of ثلاثة and is read with a dagger alif. The print leaves the two groups of slaves in apposition (“three slaves, two carrying …”) without a connecting word. شائلان, “lifting up, carrying”, is from شال, a common word in the Nights. عبيد is the plural of عبد, “slave”; in these tales it is used especially of black slaves.

sentences.t: فَحِينَ قَرُبُوا مِنَ التُّرْبَةِ قَالَ أَحَدُ الْعَبْدَيْنِ الَّذِينَ شَائِلِينَ الصُّنْدُوقَ مَالَكَ يَاصَوَابُ
sentences.tr: fa-ḥīna qarubū mina al-turbati qāla aḥadu al-ʿabdayni alladhīna shāʾilīna al-ṣundūqa mā-laka yā ṣawābu
sentences.l: So-when they-neared the-tomb-enclosure, said one of-the-two-slaves who carrying the-chest: What-to-you, O Ṣawāb?
sentences.i: And when they drew near the enclosure, one of the two slaves who carried the chest said, “What ails you, Ṣawāb?”
sentences.n: Two non-Classical forms here: الذين used for the dual (Classical اللذان or اللذين), and شائلين in the oblique ending, after a relative that has no verb, where Classical would have the nominative شائلان. Both are normal Middle Arabic; read on. مالك يا صواب (“what is the matter with you?”) is printed with مالك as a single word.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْعَبْدُ الْآخَرُ مِنْهُمَا مَالَكَ يَا كَافُورُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ʿabdu al-ākharu minhumā mā-laka yā kāfūru
sentences.l: So-said the-slave the-other of-the-two: What-to-you, O Kāfūr?
sentences.i: Said the other of the two, “And what ails you, Kāfūr?”
sentences.n: Slave names such as Ṣawāb (“Right”), Kāfūr (“Camphor”) and Bukhayt (“Little Luck”) are typical of the Nights. الآخر is printed with the precomposed آ and kept.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ أَمَا كُنَّا هُنَا وَقْتَ الْعِشَاءِ وَخَلَّيْنَا الْبَابَ مَفْتُوحًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu amā kunnā hunā waqta al-ʿishāʾi wa-khallaynā al-bāba maftūḥan
sentences.l: So-he-said to-him: Were-we-not here at-the-time of-the-evening, and-we-left the-door open?
sentences.i: Then he said to him, “Were we not here at suppertime, and did we not leave the door open?”
sentences.n: خلينا is the colloquial form II, “we left (it)”, from خلا; Classical would use تركنا. أما here opens a question that expects the answer yes, which the next speaker gives. The print does not make clear which of the two slaves speaks each time; the reading follows the sense.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ نَعَمْ هَٰذَا الْكَلَامُ صَحِيحٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla naʿam hādhā al-kalāmu ṣaḥīḥun
sentences.l: So-he-said: Yes, this the-speech true.
sentences.i: He said, “Yes, that is true.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ هَاهُوَ مَغْلُوقٌ مُتَرْبَسٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla hā-huwa maghlūqun mutarbasun
sentences.l: So-he-said: Here-it, locked, bolted.
sentences.i: Then he said, “Yet here it is, locked and bolted!”
sentences.n: متربس is obscure. It looks like a colloquial participle for “bolted, barred”, probably from a word for a bolt or bar (Persian-derived مترس / متراس or a related colloquial form); this is a guess, so the pointing مُتَرْبَسٌ is tentative.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُمَا الثَّالِثُ وَهُوَ حَامِلُ الْفَأْسِ وَالنُّورِ وَكَانَ اسْمُهُ بُخَيْتًا مَا أَقَلَّ عَقْلَكُمَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahumā al-thālithu wa-huwa ḥāmilu al-faʾsi wa-al-nūri wa-kāna ismuhu bukhaytan mā aqalla ʿaqlakumā
sentences.l: So-said to-the-two the-third, and-he the-bearer of-the-axe and-the-light, and-was his-name Bukhayt: How little your-two-sense!
sentences.i: Then the third, who bore the axe and the light, and whose name was Bukhayt, said to them, “How little sense you two have!”
sentences.n: ما أقلّ عقلكما is the wonder form: “how little your wits are!”. بخيت is the diminutive of بخت, “luck”; here it is read as the accusative Bukhaytan, since it is the predicate of كان.

sentences.t: أَمَا تَعْرِفَانِ أَنَّ أَصْحَابَ الْغِيطَانِ يَخْرُجُونَ مِنْ بَغْدَادَ وَيَرْعَوْنَ هُنَا فَيُمْسِي عَلَيْهِمُ الْمَسَاءُ فَيَدْخُلُونَ هُنَا وَيُغْلِقُونَ عَلَيْهِمُ الْبَابَ
sentences.tr: amā taʿrifāni anna aṣḥāba al-ghīṭāni yakhrujūna min baghdāda wa-yarʿawna hunā fa-yumsī ʿalayhimu al-masāʾu fa-yadkhulūna hunā wa-yughliqūna ʿalayhimu al-bāba
sentences.l: Do-you-two-not know that the-owners of-the-gardens go-out from Baghdad and-pasture here, so the-evening overtakes them, so they-enter here and-bolt on-them the-door?
sentences.i: Do you two not know that the owners of the gardens come out from Baghdad and graze their beasts here, and when evening overtakes them, they come in here and shut the door upon themselves?…
sentences.n: The speech goes on in the next unit, so this sentence is a fragment (the “…” in the English marks the cut). الغيطان, plural of غيط, are the plots of cultivated or grazing ground around the city; يرعون (“they graze”) leaves its object, their flocks, unspoken.

sentences.t: خَوْفًا مِنَ السُّودَانِ الَّذِينَ هُمْ مِثْلُنَا أَنْ يَأْخُذُوهُمْ وَيَشْوُوهُمْ وَيَأْ كُلُوهُمْ
sentences.tr: khawfan mina al-sūdāni alladhīna hum mithlunā an yaʾkhudhūhum wa-yashwūhum wa-yaʾ kulūhum
sentences.l: … In-fear from the-blacks, those-who they like-us, that they-take them and they-roast them and they-eat them.
sentences.i: … for fear of the black men who are like us, lest they seize them, roast them, and eat them.
sentences.n: This continues the previous sentence: the “them” of the three verbs is the garden owners, who bolt themselves in for fear of being seized, roasted and eaten by blacks like the speakers. The slaves share this dread of cannibals. The print splits the last verb into two words, ويا | كلوهم; read it as one, wa-yaʾkulūhum.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا لَهُ صَدَقْتَ وَاللَّهِ مَا فِينَا أَقَلُّ عَقْلًا مِنْكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū lahu ṣadaqta wa-allāhi mā fīnā aqallu ʿaqlan minka
sentences.l: And-they-said to-him: You-spoke-truly, and-God! Not in-us less in-mind than-you.
sentences.i: They said to him, “You have spoken truly, by God! There is none among us with less wit than you.”
sentences.n: The reply can be read as a barbed joke or simply as grudging agreement with a man who is not the cleverest of them. The sense of the Arabic is flat as printed, so no repair is attempted.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُمْ إِنَّكُمْ لَمْ تُصَدِّقُونِي حَتَّى نَدْخُلَ التُّرْبَةَ وَنَجِدَ فِيهَا أَحَدًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahum innakum lam tuṣaddiqūnī ḥattā nadkhula al-turbata wa-najida fīhā aḥadan
sentences.l: And-he-said to-them: Indeed-you not you-believe-me until we-enter the-tomb and-we-find in-it anyone.
sentences.i: He said to them, “You will not believe me until we go into the tomb and find someone there.”

sentences.t: وَأَنَا أَظُنُّ أَنَّهُ لَمَّارَأَى النُّورَ وَرَأَانَا هَرَبَ فَوْقَ النَّخْلَةِ خَوْفًا مِنَّا
sentences.tr: wa-anā aẓunnu annahu lammā raʾā al-nūra wa-raʾānā haraba fawqa al-nakhlati khawfan minnā
sentences.l: And-I I-think that-he when he-saw the-light and-he-saw-us he-fled above the-palm in-fear from-us.
sentences.i: And I think that when he saw the light and saw us, he fled up the palm tree for fear of us.
sentences.n: The print runs lammā raʾā and wa-raʾānā together as single words (لماراى، وراانا); the spaces are ours to restore in reading. The “he” is the stranger the slaves imagine hiding in the tree, and, though they do not know it, it is Ghānim.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ غَانِمٌ كَلَامَ الْعَبْدِ قَالَ فِي نَفْسِهِ يَا أَلْعَنَ الْعَبْدِ لَا سَتَرَ اللَّهُ عَلَيْكَ وَلَابِهَذَا الْعَقْلِ وَلَابِهَذِهِ الْمَعْرِفَةِ كُلِّهَا
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa ghānimun kalāma al-ʿabdi qāla fī nafsihi yā alʿana al-ʿabdi lā satara allāhu ʿalayka wa-lā bi-hādhā al-ʿaqli wa-lā bi-hādhihi al-maʿrifati kullihā
sentences.l: So-when he-heard Ghānim the-speech of-the-slave he-said in his-self: O most-accursed of-the-slave, not God-covered upon-you, and-not with-this the-intellect, and-not with-this-one the-knowledge, all-of-it.
sentences.i: When Ghānim heard the slave’s words, he said to himself, “O most accursed of slaves, may God not shield you — nor bless this wit of yours, nor all this cleverness of yours!”
sentences.n: A curse in two beats. “Lā satara allāhu ʿalayka” is a wish with a perfect verb (“may God not cover you”), and each wa-lā bi-… leaves its verb unsaid, so we supply “bless”. Ghānim is the stranger up the palm, and the slave’s sharpness is exactly what alarms him. Yā alʿana is our reading of يا العن as a vocative “most accursed (of)”.

sentences.t: لَاحَوْلَ وَلَاقُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ الْعَلِيِّ الْعَظِيمِ
sentences.tr: lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-allāhi al-ʿaliyyi al-ʿaẓīmi
sentences.l: No power and-no strength except with-God the-high the-great.
sentences.i: There is no power and no strength but in God, the High, the Great.
sentences.n: The standard cry of helplessness and submission, often called the ḥawqala. The print writes lā ḥawla and wa-lā quwwata as run-together words.

sentences.t: أَيْش بَقِيَ يُخَلِّصُنِي مِنْ هَؤُلَاءِ الْعَبِيدِ
sentences.tr: aysh baqiya yukhalliṣunī min hāʾulāʾi al-ʿabīdi
sentences.l: What remained it-delivers-me from these the-slaves?
sentences.i: What is left to deliver me from these slaves?
sentences.n: ايش is colloquial for “what?”, a contraction of أيّ شيء (“which thing?”). It is the everyday word in Middle Arabic where Classical would say ماذا. Bare Arabic: “what remains that will rescue me?”

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الَّذِينَ حَامِلِينَ الصُّنْدُوقَ قَالَا لِلَّذِي مَعَهُ الْفَاسُ تَعَلَّقْ عَلَى الْحَائِطِ وَافْتَحْ لَنَا الْبَابَ يَا بَخِيتُ
sentences.tr: thumma inna alladhīna ḥāmilīna al-ṣundūqa qālā li-alladhī maʿahu al-fāsu taʿallaq ʿalā al-ḥāʾiṭi wa-aftaḥ lanā al-bāba yā bakhītu
sentences.l: Then indeed those-who carrying the-chest they-two-said to-the-one-who with-him the-axe: Hang on the-wall and-open for-us the-door, O Bukhayt,
sentences.i: Then the two who were carrying the chest said to the one who had the axe, “Climb up the wall and open the door for us, Bukhayt.”
sentences.n: Middle Arabic agreement: a plural relative (alladhīna) goes with a participle in -īna (ḥāmilīna, “carrying”) and then a dual verb (qālā), so the print is loose and we read it as “the two carrying the chest”. Taʿallaq means literally “hang on”, here “scramble up”. Bukhayt is the diminutive of colloquial bakht, “luck”; the print spells it بخيت.

sentences.t: لِأَنَّنَا تَعِبْنَا مِنْ شَيْلِ الصُّنْدُوقِ عَلَى رِقَابِنَا فَإِذَا فَتَحْتَ لَنَا الْبَابَ لَكَ عَلَيْنَا وَاحِدٌ مِنَ الَّذِينَ نُمْسِكُهُمْ وَنَقْلِيهِ لَكَ بِيَدِي بِصَنْعَةٍ جَيِّدَةٍ بِحَيْثُ لَايَضِيعُ مِنْ دُهْنِهِ نُقْطَةٌ
sentences.tr: li-annanā taʿibnā min shayli al-ṣundūqi ʿalā riqābinā fa-idhā fataḥta lanā al-bāba laka ʿalaynā wāḥidun mina alladhīna numsikuhum wa-naqlīhi laka bi-yadī bi-ṣanʿatin jayyidatin bi-ḥaythu lā yaḍīʿu min duhnihi nuqṭatun
sentences.l: Because-we we-are-tired from carrying of-the-chest upon our-necks; so-when you-open for-us the-door, to-you upon-us one of those-whom we-seize-them, and-we-fry-him for-you with-my-hand with-craft good, so-that not is-lost from his-fat a-drop.
sentences.i: “For we are weary of carrying the chest on our necks. If you open the door for us, we owe you one of those we catch, and I will fry him for you with my own hand, so skilfully that not a drop of his fat is lost.”
sentences.n: These are cannibals, and the text says so plainly: they promise to cook a captive. Shayl (“carrying”) is colloquial, and the speaker slips from “we” to “my hand” (bi-yadī) in mid-promise. “Laka ʿalaynā” is the idiom of a debt: “you have a claim on us”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ بَخِيتُ أَنَا خَائِفٌ مِنْ شِي اِفْتَكَرْتُهُ مِنْ قِلَّةِ عَقْلِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla bakhītu anā khāʾifun min shī iftakartuhu min qillati ʿaqlī
sentences.l: And-he-said Bukhayt: I afraid of a-thing I-thought-of-it from littleness of-my-mind.
sentences.i: Bukhayt said, “I am afraid of something that has come to me, dull-witted as I am.”
sentences.n: شي is colloquial for شيء, “a thing”. Iftakartuhu is a relative clause with no relative word, normal Middle Arabic after an indefinite noun. “From the littleness of my wit” is self-mockery, a modest way to introduce an idea.

sentences.t: وَهُوَ أَنَّنَا نَرْمِى الصُّنْدُوقَ مِنْ وَرَاءِ الْبَابِ لِأَنَّهُ ذَخِيرَتُنَا
sentences.tr: wa-huwa annanā narmī al-ṣundūqa min warāʾi al-bābi li-annahu dhakhīratunā
sentences.l: And-it that-we we-throw the-chest from behind the-door, because-it our-store.
sentences.i: It is this: that we throw the chest in from beyond the door, for it is our precious store.
sentences.n: His plan is to heave the chest over rather than open the door; he is cautious about the chest because it is their stock, their treasure. Dhakhīra is stored goods, a hoard.

sentences.t: فَقَالَا لَهُ إِنْ رَمَيْنَاهُ يَنْكَسِرْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālā lahu in ramaynāhu yankasir
sentences.l: And-they-two-said to-him: If we-throw-it it-breaks.
sentences.i: They said to him, “If we throw it, it will break.”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُمَا أَنَا خَائِفٌ أَنْ يَكُونَ جَوَّالتُّرْبَةِ الْحَرَامِيَّةُ الَّذِينَ يَقْتُلُونَ النَّاسَ وَيَسْرِقُونَ الْأَشْيَاءَ لِأَنَّهُمْ إِذَا أَمْسَى عَلَيْهِمُ الْوَقْتُ يَدْخُلُونَ فِي هَذِهِ الْأَمَاكِنِ وَيَقْسِمُونَ مَايَكُونُ مَعَهُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahumā anā khāʾifun an yakūna jawwa al-turbati al-ḥarāmiyyatu alladhīna yaqtulūna al-nāsa wa-yasriqūna al-ashyāʾa li-annahum idhā amsā ʿalayhimu al-waqtu yadkhulūna fī hādhihi al-amākini wa-yaqsimūna mā yakūnu maʿahum
sentences.l: And-he-said to-them-two: I afraid that there-be inside the-tomb the-thieves, those-who they-kill the-people and-they-steal the-things, because-they when evening-came upon-them the-time they-enter in these the-places and-they-divide what is with-them.
sentences.i: Then he said to them, “I fear that thieves may be inside the tomb — the kind who kill people and steal their goods, and who, when evening overtakes them, enter places like this and share out whatever they have with them.”
sentences.n: Jawwa is the colloquial “inside”; the print runs it into the article (جوالتربة) with a single alif, and we read jawwa al-turba, “the inside of the tomb”, as an accusative adverb, with al-ḥarāmiyya (“the thieves”, colloquial plural of ḥarāmī) as the subject. The verb yakūna stays singular before a plural subject, as is usual when it comes first.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الْاِثْنَانِ الْحَامِلَانِ لِلصُّنْدُوقِ يَا قَلِيلَ الْعَقْلِ هَلْ يَقْدِرُونَ أَنْ يَدْخُلُوا هُنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-ithnāni al-ḥāmilāni li-al-ṣundūqi yā qalīla al-ʿaqli hal yaqdirūna an yadkhulū hunā
sentences.l: And-said to-him the-two the-carriers for-the-chest: O little of-the-mind! do they-are-able that they-enter here?
sentences.i: The two chest-bearers said to him, “O man of little wit, could they ever get in here?”
sentences.n: “Qalīl al-ʿaql” (“little of mind”) turns his own self-mockery back on him. Their reasoning is that the door was locked and the wall high, so no thieves could be inside.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمَا حَمَلَا الصُّنْدُوقَ وَتَعَلَّقَا عَلَى الْحَائِطِ وَنَزَلَا وَفَتَحَا الْبَابَ وَالْعَبْدُ الثَّالِثُ الَّذِي هُوَ بَخِيتُ وَاقِفٌ لَهُمَا بِالْفَانُوسِ وَالْفَاسِ وَالْمِقْطَفِ الَّذِي فِيهِ بَعْضٌ مِنَ الْجِبْسِ
sentences.tr: thumma innahumā ḥamalā al-ṣundūqa wa-taʿallaqā ʿalā al-ḥāʾiṭi wa-nazalā wa-fataḥā al-bāba wa-al-ʿabdu al-thālithu alladhī huwa bakhītu wāqifun lahumā bi-al-fānūsi wa-al-fāsi wa-al-miqṭafi alladhī fīhi baʿḍun mina al-jibsi
sentences.l: Then indeed-they-two they-lifted the-chest and-they-clung on the-wall and-they-descended and-they-opened the-door, and-the-slave the-third, who he Bukhayt, standing for-them with-the-lantern and-the-axe and-the-basket which in-it some of-the-plaster.
sentences.i: Then the two lifted the chest, scrambled up the wall, dropped down and opened the door, while the third slave, Bakhīt, stood by them with the lantern, the axe, and the basket that held some plaster.
sentences.n: The gypsum plaster (jibs) is for sealing the tomb again once the chest is buried. The wāw of wa-al-ʿabdu is circumstantial: it marks something happening at the same moment.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ جَلَسُوا وَقَفَلُوا الْبَابَ
sentences.tr: thumma innahum jalasū wa-qafalū al-bāba
sentences.l: Then indeed-they they-sat and-they-locked the-door.
sentences.i: Then the three sat down and locked the door.
sentences.n: They lock the door behind them, so the hidden Ghānim is now shut in with the three slaves.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَاحِدٌ مِنْهُمْ يَا إِخْوَتِي نَحْنُ تَعِبْنَا مِنَ الْمَشْيِ وَالشَّيْلِ وَالْحَطِّ وَفَتْحِ الْبَابِ وَقَفْلِهِ وَهَذَا الْوَقْتُ نِصْفُ اللَّيْلِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wāḥidun minhum yā ikhwatī naḥnu taʿibnā mina al-mashyi wa-al-shayli wa-al-ḥaṭṭi wa-fatḥi al-bābi wa-qaflihi wa-hādhā al-waqtu niṣfu al-layli
sentences.l: And-said one of-them: O my-brothers, we we-are-tired from the-walking and-the-carrying and-the-setting-down and-opening of-the-door and-locking-of-it; and-this the-time half of-the-night,
sentences.i: One of them said, “My brothers, we are weary with walking and carrying and setting down, with opening the door and locking it, and now it is the middle of the night,
sentences.n: Shayl is colloquial “carrying” and ḥaṭṭ is “putting down”. The sentence continues in the next unit.

sentences.t: وَلَابَقِيَ فِينَا نَفَسٌ نَفْتَحُ التُّرْبَةَ وَنَدْفِنُ الصُّنْدُوقَ
sentences.tr: wa-lā baqiya fīnā nafasun naftaḥu al-turbata wa-nadfinu al-ṣundūqa
sentences.l: And-not remained in-us breath we-open the-tomb and-we-bury the-chest,
sentences.i: and we have no breath left to open the tomb and bury the chest;
sentences.n: Another relative clause with no relative word: “no breath remains in us (with which) we might open the tomb”.

sentences.t: وَلَكِنْ حَتَّى نَرْتَاحَ ثَلَٰثَ سَاعَاتٍ ثُمَّ نَقُومَ وَنَقْضِيَ حَاجَتَنَا
sentences.tr: wa-lākin ḥattā nartāḥa thalātha sāʿātin thumma naqūma wa-naqḍiya ḥājatanā
sentences.l: But until we-rest three hours, then we-rise and-we-accomplish our-need,
sentences.i: but let us rest three hours, then rise and do what we came to do,
sentences.n: The print has ثلث for ثلاث (“three”), without the alif; we mark the missing long ā with a dagger alif. Ḥattā with the subjunctive here means “let us rest until…”, a proposal rather than a purpose.

sentences.t: وَكُلُّ وَاحِدٍ مِنَّا يَحْكِي
sentences.tr: wa-kullu wāḥidin minnā yaḥkī
sentences.l: And-every one of-us he-tells …
sentences.i: and each one of us shall tell …
sentences.n: The sentence is left open here: what each one is to tell (his own story) follows in the next unit.

sentences.t: لَنَا عَلَى سَبَبِ تَطْوِيشِهِ وَجَمِيعِ مَا وَقَعَ لَهُ مِنَ الْمُبْتَدَأِ إِلَى الْمُنْتَهَى لِأَجْلِ فَوَاتِ هَذِهِ اللَّيْلَةِ وَنَأْخُذُ لَنَا رَاحَةً
sentences.tr: lanā ʿalā sababi taṭwīshihi wa-jamīʿi mā waqaʿa lahu mina al-mubtadaʾi ilā al-muntahā li-ajli fawāti hādhihi al-laylati wa-naʾkhudhu lanā rāḥatan
sentences.l: … for-us, upon the cause of his eunuch-making and all that befell him, from the beginning to the end, for the sake of the passing of this night, and we take for-ourselves rest.
sentences.i: … to us the reason he was made a eunuch, and all that befell him from first to last, so that this night may slip by and we may take our ease.
sentences.n: This sentence completes the previous one, so the verb that governs “for us” (presumably “tell”) is left unspoken. The “his” in “his being made a eunuch” stands for each member of the company in turn. The verb in “and we take” is left in the indicative, as the print gives it; Classical grammar might expect a subjunctive after “so that”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْأَوَّلُ الَّذِي كَانَ حَامِلَ الْفَانُوسِ وَاسْمُهُ بَخِيتٌ أَنَا أَحْكِي لَكُمْ حِكَايَتِي
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-awwalu alladhī kāna ḥāmila al-fānūsi wa-ismuhu bakhītun anā aḥkī lakum ḥikāyatī
sentences.l: And said the first, who was bearer-of the lantern, and his-name (was) Bukhayt: I tell to-you my-tale.
sentences.i: Then the first, the one who had carried the lantern, whose name was Bukhayt, said, “I will tell you my story.”
sentences.n: Bukhayt means “fortunate, lucky”, which sits grimly beside what he is about to tell. The Arabic uses the plain present, أحكي “I tell”, for what English phrases as a promise.

sentences.t: فَقَالُوا لَهُ تَالَمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qālū lahu tālam
sentences.l: And they-said to-him: speak!
sentences.i: They said to him, “Speak.”
sentences.n: The print has تالم, which is not a word. It looks like a slip for تكلم takallam, “speak”, one letter off, and I translate it so; the pointing here follows the letters as printed.

sentences.t: قَالَ لَهُمْ يَا إِخْوَتِي اعْلَمُوا أَنِّي لَمَّا كُنْتُ صَغِيرٌ أَجَاءَ بِي الْجَلَّابُ مِنْ بَلَدِي
sentences.tr: qāla lahum yā ikhwatī iʿlamū annī lammā kuntu ṣaghīrun ajāʾa bī al-jallābu min baladī
sentences.l: He said to them: O my-brothers, know that I, when I was small, brought-me the slave-dealer from my country.
sentences.i: He said to them, “My brothers, know that when I was small, a slave-dealer carried me off from my homeland.”
sentences.n: The print has صغير with no alif, i.e. the bare uninflected predicate of Middle Arabic where Classical would write صغيرًا; I have pointed it as printed. أجاء is the fourth form of جاء; the ordinary phrase would be جاء بي “brought me”, and the sense is the same. الجلاب is the dealer who brings slaves in from abroad to sell.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ عُمْرِي خَمْسَ سِنِينَ فَبَاعَنِي لِوَاحِدٍ جَاوِيشٍ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna ʿumrī khamsa sinīna fa-bāʿanī li-wāḥidin jāwīshin
sentences.l: And my-age was five years, and he-sold-me to one, a sergeant.
sentences.i: I was five years old, and he sold me to a certain sergeant.
sentences.n: جاويش is the Turkish çavuş, a sergeant or petty officer. After a number the print uses the plural in -īna (سنين), as the spoken language does; Classical would say خمس سنوات.

sentences.t: وَكَانَ لَهُ بِنْتٌ عُمْرُهَا ثَلَٰثَ سِنِينَ
sentences.tr: wa-kāna lahu bintun ʿumruhā thalātha sinīna
sentences.l: And there-was to-him a daughter, her-age three years.
sentences.i: He had a daughter who was three years old.
sentences.n: ثلث is printed for ثلاث, with the long ā unwritten; the dagger alif marks it.

sentences.t: فَتَرَبَّيْتُ مَعَهَا وَهُمْ يَضْحَكُونَ عَلَيَّ وَأَنَا أُلَاعِبُ الْبِنْتَ وَأَرْقُصُ لَهَا وَأُغَنِّي لَهَا إِلَى أَنْ صَارَ عُمْرِي اثْنَىْ عَشَرَ سَنَةً وَهِيَ بِنْتٌ
sentences.tr: fa-tarabbaytu maʿahā wa-hum yaḍḥakūna ʿalayya wa-anā ulāʿibu al-binta wa-arquṣu lahā wa-ughannī lahā ilā an ṣāra ʿumrī ithnay ʿashara sanatan wa-hiya bintun
sentences.l: So I-was-raised with-her, while they laugh at me, and I play-with the girl and dance for-her and sing for-her, until my-age became twelve years, and she a girl […]
sentences.i: So I grew up beside her, with the household laughing over me as I played with the girl, danced for her and sang to her, until I was twelve years old, and she still a girl […]
sentences.n: A passage is skipped here for now.

sentences.t: لِمَحَبَّتِهِمْ لِي
sentences.tr: li-maḥabbatihim lī
sentences.l: […] for-their-love for-me.
sentences.i: […] out of their fondness for me.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ أُمَّهَا خَطَبَتْ لَهَا شَابًّا مُزَيِّنًا كَانَ يُزَيِّنُ أَبَاهَا
sentences.tr: thumma inna ummahā khaṭabat lahā shābban muzayyinan kāna yuzayyinu abāhā
sentences.l: Then indeed her-mother sought-in-marriage for-her a youth, a barber, who used-to groom her-father.
sentences.i: Then her mother arranged a match for her with a young barber who used to trim her father’s hair and beard.
sentences.n: مزين is “barber” (one who makes the head and face neat), and the next verb يزين is the same word as a verb. The mother acts for her daughter, and the father is kept out of it.

sentences.t: وَأَمْهَرَتْهَا مِنْ عِنْدِهَا وَجَهَّزَتْهَا لَهُ كُلَّ هَذَا وَأَبُوهَا لَا يَعْلَمُ بِحَالِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-amharathā min ʿindihā wa-jahhazathā lahu kulla hādhā wa-abūhā lā yaʿlamu bi-ḥālihā
sentences.l: And she-paid-the-bride-price-for-her from at-her (own funds) and outfitted-her for-him, all this while her-father knows not of her state.
sentences.i: She paid the bride-price for her out of her own purse and fitted her out for him, and all the while her father knew nothing of her condition.
sentences.n: Here it is the mother who pays the مهر, normally the groom’s gift to the bride. “Her condition” (حالها) means that the girl was no longer a virgin, as the wedding-night trick below makes plain.

sentences.t: وَصَارُوا يَجْتَهِدُونَ فِي تَحْصِيلِ جِهَازِهَا
sentences.tr: wa-ṣārū yajtahidūna fī taḥṣīli jihāzihā
sentences.l: And they-became striving in the procuring of-her trousseau.
sentences.i: And they set about earnestly gathering her trousseau.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّهُمْ أَمْسَكُونِي عَلَى غَفْلَةٍ وَطَوَّشُونِي
sentences.tr: thumma innahum amsakūnī ʿalā ghaflatin wa-ṭawwashūnī
sentences.l: Then indeed they seized-me upon heedlessness and eunuch-made-me.
sentences.i: Then they seized me unawares and made a eunuch of me.
sentences.n: طوّش is a verb built on the noun طواشي, “eunuch”, a Turkish and Persian loan; the print’s shadda on the waw is kept.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا زَفُّوهَا لِلْعَرِيسِ جَعَلُونِي طَوَّاشِيًّا لَهَا أَمْشِي قُدَّ امَهَا أَيْنَمَا رَاحَتْ سَوَاءٌ كَانَ رَوَاحُهَا إِلَى الْحَمَّامِ أَوْ بَيْتِ أَبِيهَا
sentences.tr: wa-lammā zaffūhā li-al-ʿarīsi jaʿalūnī ṭawwāshiyyan lahā amshī qudd āmahā aynamā rāḥat sawāʾun kāna rawāḥuhā ilā al-ḥammāmi aw bayti abīhā
sentences.l: And when they-conducted-her-in-procession to-the-bridegroom, they-made-me a eunuch-attendant for-her; I walk before-her wherever she went, whether her going was to the bath or the house of-her-father.
sentences.i: And when they led her in procession to the bridegroom, they made me her eunuch attendant, and I walked ahead of her wherever she went, whether to the bath or to her father’s house.
sentences.n: The print writes قدامها as two words, قد امها; I point it as one word, quddāmahā, “in front of her”. The alternative, “in front of her mother”, would make the bride’s mother part of the escort, and the sense is much the same. A طواشي is the eunuch who guards and escorts a lady.

sentences.t: وَقَدْ سَتَرُوا أَمْرَهَا
sentences.tr: wa-qad satarū amrahā
sentences.l: And indeed they-concealed her matter.
sentences.i: They had hushed up her affair.

sentences.t: وَلَيْلَةَ الدُّخْلَةِ ذَبَحُوا عَلَيٰ قَمِيصِهَا فَرْخَ حَمَامَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-laylata al-dukhlati dhabaḥū ʿalā qamīṣihā farkha ḥamāmatin
sentences.l: And the night-of the entering they-slaughtered upon her shift a chick of-a-dove.
sentences.i: And on the wedding night they slit the throat of a young pigeon over her shift.
sentences.n: This is the old trick: the pigeon’s blood on the shift stands in for the blood of a virgin bride. The print spells على with a dotted ya, علي, here (ʿalā), the same letters as عليّ “at me” a few lines earlier; the dagger alif marks the difference. الدخلة is “the going-in”, the consummation night.

sentences.t: وَمَكَثْتُ أَنَا عِنْدَهَا مُدَّةً طَوِيلَةً وَأَنَا أَتَمَلَّى بِحُسْنِهَا وَجَمَا لَهَا مِنْ بَوْسٍ وَعِنَاقٍ وَرُقَادٍ
sentences.tr: wa-makathtu anā ʿindahā muddatan ṭawīlatan wa-anā atamallā bi-ḥusnihā wa-jamā lahā min bawsin wa-ʿināqin wa-ruqādin
sentences.l: And I-stayed I with-her a long period, while I take-my-fill by her beauty and her-loveliness, in kissing and embracing and lying-down.
sentences.i: And I stayed with her a long while, taking my fill of her beauty and her loveliness, in kisses, embraces and nights beside her.
sentences.n: The print splits جمالها as جما لها. تملّى بـ is “to enjoy to the full”. بوس “kissing” is a Persian-derived word of the spoken language. رقاد is lying down to sleep, here beside her.

sentences.t: إِلَى أَنْ مَاتَتْ هِيَ وَزَوْجُهَا وَأُمُّهَا وَأَبُوهَا
sentences.tr: ilā an mātat hiya wa-zawjuhā wa-ummuhā wa-abūhā
sentences.l: Until died she and her-husband and her-mother and her-father.
sentences.i: Until she died, and her husband, and her mother, and her father.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ أَخَذُونِي لِبَيْتِ الْمَالِ وَصِرْتُ فِي هَذَا الْمَكَانِ وَقَدِ ارْتَفَقْتُ بِكُمْ
sentences.tr: thumma akhadhūnī li-bayti al-māli wa-ṣirtu fī hādhā al-makāni wa-qadi irtafaqtu bikum
sentences.l: Then they-took-me to the house of-the wealth, and I-became in this place, and I-have found-comfort in-you.
sentences.i: Then they took me to the public treasury, and I came to be in this place, where I have found comfort in your company.
sentences.n: بيت المال, “the house of wealth”, is the public treasury, to which a slave with no heir passed. ارتفق بـ is “to take comfort or benefit from”.

sentences.t: وَهَذَا يَا إِخْوَتِي سَبَبُ قَطْعِ إِحْلِيلِي وَالسَّلَامُ
sentences.tr: wa-hādhā yā ikhwatī sababu qaṭʿi iḥlīlī wa-al-salāmu
sentences.l: And this, O my-brothers, (is) the cause of the cutting-off of-my urethra, and the peace.
sentences.i: And that, my brothers, is the reason my member was cut away; and that is all.
sentences.n: إحليل strictly means the urethra, the passage; here it stands for the organ itself. والسلام, “and peace”, is the usual closing word, “and that is the end of it”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ الْعَبْدُ الثَّانِي اعْلَمُوا يَا إِخْوَتِي أَنِّي كُنْتُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-ʿabdu al-thānī iʿlamū yā ikhwatī annī kuntu
sentences.l: And said the slave, the second: Know, O my-brothers, that I was …
sentences.i: Then the second slave said, “My brothers, know that I was …”
sentences.n: The sentence breaks off here; the second slave’s tale goes on in the next unit.

sentences.t: فِي ابْتِدَاءِ أَمْرِي وَأَنَا ابْنُ ثَمَانِ سِنِينَ أَكْذِبُ عَلَى الْجَلَّابَةِ كُلَّ سَنَةٍ كَذْبَةً حَتَّى يَقَعُوا فِي بَعْضِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fī ibtidāʾi amrī wa-anā ibnu thamāni sinīna akdhibu ʿalā al-jallābati kulla sanatin kadhbatan ḥattā yaqaʿū fī baʿḍihim
sentences.l: In beginning-of my-affair, and-I son-of eight years, I-lie upon the slave-dealers every year a-lie, until they-fall in one-another…
sentences.i: In the beginning of my story, when I was a boy of eight, I told the slave-dealers a lie every year, until they fell out with one another…
sentences.n: The second slave’s own tale begins here, and the sentence runs on into the next unit, hence the dots. The speaker is the slave later called Kāfūr. ثمان is the colloquial form of ثماني, “eight”. The verb يقعوا has lost its final nūn after حتى, as Classical grammar requires, and means “fall among one another”.

sentences.t: فَقَلِقَ مِنِّي الْجَلَّابُ وَأَنْزَلَنِي فِي يَدِ الدَّلَّالِ وَأَمَرَهُ أَنْ يُنَادِيَ مَنْ يَشْتَرِ هَٰذَا الْعَبْدَ عَلَى عَيْبِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qaliqa minnī al-jallābu wa-anzalanī fī yadi al-dallāli wa-amarahu an yunādiya man yashtari hādhā al-ʿabda ʿalā ʿaybihi
sentences.l: And-he-was-uneasy from-me, the slave-dealer, and-he-made-me-descend into hand-of the crier, and-commanded-him that he-cry: “Whoever buys this slave upon his-fault…”
sentences.i: The dealer grew uneasy on my account and put me into the hands of an auctioneer, bidding him cry: “Who will buy this slave, fault and all?”
sentences.n: الدلال is the broker or auctioneer who cries the goods. يشتر (for يشتري) is the jussive after مَن, “whoever”, and the crier’s cry is meant as a call, not a question.

sentences.t: فَقِيلَ لَهُ وَمَا عَيْبُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qīla lahu wa-mā ʿaybuhu
sentences.l: And-it-was-said to-him: “And what [is] his-fault?”
sentences.i: Then someone asked him, “And what is his fault?”

sentences.t: قَالَ يَكْذِبُ كُلَّ سَنَةٍ كَذْبَةً وَاحِدَةً
sentences.tr: qāla yakdhibu kulla sanatin kadhbatan wāḥidatan
sentences.l: He-said: He-lies every year one lie.
sentences.i: “He tells one lie every year,” he answered.

sentences.t: فَتَقَدَّمَ رَجُلٌ تَاجِرٌ إِلَى الدَّلَّالِ وَقَالَ لِلدَّلَّالِ كَمْ أَعْطَوْا فِيهِ مِنَ الثَّمَنِ عَلَى عَيْبِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-taqaddama rajulun tājirun ilā al-dallāli wa-qāla li-al-dallāli kam aʿṭaw fīhi min al-thamani ʿalā ʿaybihi
sentences.l: And-he-stepped-forward a-man, a-merchant, to the crier, and-he-said to-the-crier: How-much gave-they in him of the price upon his-fault?
sentences.i: Then a merchant stepped up to the crier and asked him, “What price have they offered for him, fault and all?”

sentences.t: قَالَ أَعْطَوْا سِتُّمِائَةِ دِرْهَمٍ
sentences.tr: qāla aʿṭaw sittumiʾati dirhamin
sentences.l: He-said: They-gave six-hundred-of dirham.
sentences.i: “They have offered six hundred dirhams,” said the crier.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ وَلَكَ عِشْرُونَ دِرْهَمًا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla wa-laka ʿishrūna dirhaman
sentences.l: And-he-said: And-to-you twenty dirham.
sentences.i: The merchant said, “And twenty dirhams for you.”
sentences.n: The twenty dirhams are the crier’s brokerage (دلالة), which he collects a few lines on.

sentences.t: فَجَمَعَ بَيْنَهُ وَبَيْنَ الْجَلَّابِ وَقَبَضَ مِنْهُ الدَّرَاهِمَ وَأَوْصَلَنِي الدَّلَّالُ إِلَى مَنْزِلِ ذَٰلِكَ التَّاجِرِ وَأَخَذَ دَلَالَتَهُ وَانْصَرَفَ
sentences.tr: fa-jamaʿa baynahu wa-bayna al-jallābi wa-qabaḍa minhu al-darāhima wa-awṣalanī al-dallālu ilā manzili dhālika al-tājiri wa-akhadha dalālatahu wa-inṣarafa
sentences.l: And-he-joined between-him and-between the slave-dealer, and-took from-him the dirhams, and-made-me-arrive the crier to house-of that merchant, and-took his-crying-fee, and-departed.
sentences.i: He brought the merchant and the dealer together, and took the money from the merchant’s hand; then the crier conducted me to that merchant’s house, collected his fee, and went his way.

sentences.t: فَكَسَانِي هَٰذَا التَّاجِرُ مَا يُنَا سِبُنِي مِنَ الْقُمَاشِ وَصِرْتُ عِنْدَهُ أَخْدُمُهُ بَاقِيَ سَنَتِي إِلَى أَنْ هَلَّتِ السَّنَةُ الْجَدِيدَةُ بِالْخَيْرِ وَكَانَتْ سَنَةً مُبَارَكَةً مُخْصِبَةً بِالنَّبَاتِ
sentences.tr: fa-kasānī hādhā al-tājiru mā yunā sibunī min al-qumāshi wa-ṣirtu ʿindahu akhdumuhu bāqiya sanatī ilā an hallati al-sanatu al-jadīdatu bi-al-khayri wa-kānat sanatan mubārakatan mukhṣibatan bi-al-nabāti
sentences.l: And-he-clothed-me this merchant what suits-me of the cloth, and-I-became at-him I-serve-him remainder-of my-year until came-new the year the new with-the good, and-it-was a-year blessed, fertile with-the plants.
sentences.i: This merchant clothed me in whatever cloth suited me, and I stayed with him, serving him for the rest of my year, until the new year came in with good fortune: a blessed year, rich with growing things.
sentences.n: In the print, ما يناسبني (“what suits me”) is broken into two pieces, ينا and سبني; they are pointed here as the one word يُنَاسِبُنِي. Note هلت, “came in”, said of a new moon or a new season; here it is the new year.

sentences.t: فَصَارَ التُّجَّارُ يَعْمَلُونَ كُلَّ يَوْمٍ عَزُومَةً وَفِي كُلِّ يَوْمٍ عَلَى وَاحِدٍ مِنْهُمْ إِلَى أَنْ جَاتِ الْعَزُومَةُ عَلَى سَيِّدِي فِي غَيْطِ بَرَّالْبَلَدِ
sentences.tr: fa-ṣāra al-tujjāru yaʿmalūna kulla yawmin ʿazūmatan wa-fī kulli yawmin ʿalā wāḥidin minhum ilā an jāti al-ʿazūmatu ʿalā sayyidī fī ghayṭi barra al-baladi
sentences.l: And-became the merchants they-make every day an-invitation, and-in every day upon one of-them, until came the invitation upon my-master in field-of outside-of the town.
sentences.i: The merchants fell to giving feasts, one each day, each day at the house of a different man, until the turn of the invitation came to my master, at a garden outside the town.
sentences.n: Middle Arabic: عزومة (for the Classical عزيمة or دعوة) is the Egyptian word for a banquet, and غيط (Egyptian, for Classical حقل) means a field or garden-plot. جات is the colloquial spelling of جاءت, “she came”. بر البلد, “outside the town”, is printed as one word. Here على is “at the expense of, at the house of”.

sentences.t: فَرَاحَ هُوَ وَالتُّجَّارُ إِلَى الْبُسْتَانِ وَأَخَذَ لَهُمْ جَمِيعَ مَا يَحْتَاجُونَ إِلَيْهِ مِنْ أَكْلٍ وَغَيْرِهِ
sentences.tr: fa-rāḥa huwa wa-al-tujjāru ilā al-bustāni wa-akhadha lahum jamīʿa mā yaḥtājūna ilayhi min aklin wa-ghayrihi
sentences.l: And-he-went, he and-the merchants, to the orchard, and-took for-them all that they-need to-it, of food and-other-than-it.
sentences.i: He went with the merchants to the orchard, and took along everything they would need, food and the rest.

sentences.t: فَجَلَسُوا يَأْ كُلُونَ وَيَشْرَبُونَ وَيَتَنَادَمُونَ إِلَى وَقْتِ الظُّهْرِ
sentences.tr: fa-jalasū ya-ʾkulūna wa-yashrabūna wa-yatanādamūna ilā waqti al-ẓuhri
sentences.l: And-they-sat they-eat and-they-drink and-they-carouse until time-of the noon.
sentences.i: They sat eating and drinking and keeping one another company over the cups until the noon hour.
sentences.n: The print divides يأكلون into يا and كلون; it is pointed here as the one word يَأْكُلُونَ.

sentences.t: فَاحْتَاجَ سَيِّدِي إِلَى مَصْلَحَةٍ مِنَ الْبَيْتِ فَقَالَ لِي يَا عَبْدُ ارْكَبِ الْبَغْلَةَ وَرُحْ إِلَى الْمَنْزِلِ وَهَاتِ مِنْ سِتِّكَ الْحَاجَةَ الْفُلَانِيَّةَ وَارْجِعْ بِسُرْعَةٍ
sentences.tr: fa-iḥtāja sayyidī ilā maṣlaḥatin min al-bayti fa-qāla lī yā ʿabdu irkabi al-baghlata wa-ruḥ ilā al-manzili wa-hāti min sittika al-ḥājata al-fulāniyyata wa-irjiʿ bi-surʿatin
sentences.l: And-he-needed my-master to a-need from the house, and-he-said to-me: O slave, ride the mule, and-go to the house, and-bring from your-lady the thing, the so-and-so, and-return with-speed.
sentences.i: My master found he needed something from the house, and said to me, “Slave, mount the mule and ride home; ask your mistress for such-and-such a thing, and come back quickly.”
sentences.n: ست (sitt, “lady”) is the colloquial word for a mistress of the house; ستك is “your lady” and ستي below is “my lady”. مصلحة here is “something needed, an errand”.

sentences.t: فَامْتَثَلْتُ أَمْرَهُ وَرُحْتُ إِلَى الْمَنْزِلِ فَلَمَّا قَرُبْتُ مِنَ الْمَنْزِلِ صَرَخْتُ وَأَرْخَيْتُ الدُّمُوعَ
sentences.tr: fa-imtathaltu amrahu wa-ruḥtu ilā al-manzili fa-lammā qarubtu min al-manzili ṣarakhtu wa-arkhaytu al-dumūʿa
sentences.l: And-I-complied-with his-command and-went to the house; and-when I-drew-near from the house I-cried-out and-loosed the tears.
sentences.i: I did as he bade me and rode to the house; and when I drew near it, I cried out and let my tears run free.

sentences.t: فَاجْتَمَعَ عَلَيَّ أَهْلُ الْحَارَةِ كِبَارًا وَصِغَارًا
sentences.tr: fa-ijtamaʿa ʿalayya ahlu al-ḥārati kibāran wa-ṣighāran
sentences.l: And-gathered upon me the people-of the quarter, big-ones and-small-ones.
sentences.i: The people of the quarter gathered around me, great and small.

sentences.t: وَسَمِعَتْ حِسِّي زَوْجَةُ سَيِّدِي وَبَنَاتُهُ فَفَتَحُوالِي الْبَابَ وَسَأَلُونِي عَنِ الْخَمْرِ
sentences.tr: wa-samiʿat ḥissī zawjatu sayyidī wa-banātuhu fa-fataḥū lī al-bāba wa-saʾalūnī ʿani al-khamri
sentences.l: And-heard my-sound the wife-of my-master and-his-daughters, and-they-opened to-me the door, and-asked-me about the wine.
sentences.i: My master’s wife and daughters heard my voice, and opened the door to me, and asked me for the news.
sentences.n: The print has الخمر (“the wine”) where the sense plainly calls for الخبر (“the news”): a compositor’s slip. It is pointed as printed, and the idiomatic line gives the sense. The verb سمعت is feminine singular though followed by the wife and the daughters, a normal Arabic agreement with the nearer subject. ففتحوالي, “and they opened to me”, is printed as one word.

sentences.t: فَقُلْتُ لَهُمْ أَنَّ سَيِّدِي كَانَ جَالِسًا تَحْتَ حَائِظٍ قَدِيمَةٍ هُوَ وَأَصْحَابُهُ فَوَقَعَتْ عَلَيْهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-qultu lahum anna sayyidī kāna jālisan taḥta ḥāʾiẓin qadīmatin huwa wa-aṣḥābuhu fa-waqaʿat ʿalayhim
sentences.l: And-I-said to-them: That my-master was sitting under a-wall, an-old-one, he and-his-companions, and-it-fell upon-them.
sentences.i: I told them, “My master was sitting beneath an old wall with his companions, and it fell on them.”
sentences.n: Here حائظ (for حائط) is treated as feminine, as in قديمة and وقعت; the lie is told with a straight face.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَأَيْتُ مَا جَرَى لَهُمْ رَكِبْتُ الْبَغْلَةَ وَجِئْتُ مُسْرِعًا لِأُخْبِرَكُمْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾaytu mā jarā lahum rakibtu al-baghlata wa-jiʾtu musriʿan li-ukhbirakum
sentences.l: And-when I-saw what happened to-them, I-rode the mule and-came hastening in-order-to-inform-you.
sentences.i: When I saw what had befallen them, I mounted the mule and came in haste to tell you.
sentences.n: The lām of لأخبركم means “in order to”: li-ukhbirakum, “so as to tell you”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا سَمِعَ بَنَانُهُ وَزَوْجَنُهُ ذَٰلِكَ صَرَخُوا وَشَقُّوا ثِيَابَهُمْ وَلَطَمُوا عَلَى وُجُوهِهِمْ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā samiʿa banānuhu wa-zawjanuhu dhālika ṣarakhū wa-shaqqū thiyābahum wa-laṭamū ʿalā wujūhihim
sentences.l: And-when heard his-daughters and-his-wife that, they-cried-out and-tore their-garments and-struck upon their-faces.
sentences.i: When his daughters and his wife heard this, they screamed, and tore their clothes, and beat their faces.
sentences.n: The print has بنانه وزوجنه, with a nūn in place of the tāʾ, for بناته وزوجته (“his daughters and his wife”); an evident slip, kept as printed in the Arabic and pointed to match, while the translation follows the sense. The verb سمع is singular before its plural subject, which is regular.

sentences.t: فَانَتْ إِلَيْهِمُ الْجِيرَانُ
sentences.tr: fa-anat ilayhimu al-jīrānu
sentences.l: And-[came] to-them the neighbours.
sentences.i: Then the neighbours came to them.
sentences.n: The form فانت is probably a misprint for فأتت or فاتت, “and she came”, with the same nūn for tāʾ as in the line above; it is pointed as printed and translated by the sense. The verb is feminine because جيران is a collective plural.

sentences.t: وَأَمَّا زَوْجَةُ سَيِّدِي فَإِنَّهَا قَلَبَتْ مَتَاعَ الْبَيْتِ بَعْضَهُ عَلَى بَعْضٍ وَأَخْرَبَتْ رُفُوفَهُ وَكَسَرَتْ طَيْقَانَهُ وَشَبَابِيكَهُ وَسَخَّمَتْ حِيطَانَهُ بِطِينٍ وَنِيلَةٍ
sentences.tr: wa-ammā zawjatu sayyidī fa-innahā qalabat matāʿa al-bayti baʿḍahu ʿalā baʿḍin wa-akhrabat rufūfahu wa-kasarat ṭayqānahu wa-shabābīkahu wa-sakhkhamat ḥīṭānahu bi-ṭīnin wa-nīlatin
sentences.l: And-as-for the wife-of my-master, so-indeed-she overturned goods-of the house, some-of-it upon some, and-ruined its-shelves, and-broke its-niches and-its-windows, and-blackened its-walls with-mud and-indigo.
sentences.i: As for my master’s wife, she turned the household goods upside down, one heap on another, wrecked the shelves, smashed the wall-niches and the windows, and smeared the walls with mud and indigo.
sentences.n: Egyptian vocabulary: طيقان is the plural of طاقة, a niche in the wall; شبابيك is the plural of شباك, “window”; and نيلة is indigo, the blue dye used here as a mark of mourning.

sentences.t: وَقَالَتْ لِي وَيْلَكَ يَا كَافُورُ تَعَالَ سَاعِدْنِي وَأَخْرِبْ هَٰذِهِ الدَّوَالِيبَ وَكَسِّرْ هَٰذِهِ الأَوَانِيَ وَالصِّينِيَّ وَغَيْرَهُ
sentences.tr: wa-qālat lī waylaka yā kāfūru taʿāla sāʿidnī wa-akhrib hādhihi al-dawālība wa-kassir hādhihi al-awāniya wa-al-ṣīniyya wa-ghayrahu
sentences.l: And-she-said to-me: Woe-to-you, O Kāfūr! Come, help-me, and-ruin these cupboards, and-smash these vessels and-the china and-the-rest.
sentences.i: And she said to me, “Woe to you, Kāfūr! Come and help me: ruin these cupboards, smash these vessels and the china and the rest!”
sentences.n: Kāfūr (“camphor”) is the slave’s name, a common one for black slaves in the Nights; the speaker of this tale is therefore a slave called Kāfūr. The pronoun in وغيره is masculine singular for “the rest”, as colloquial usage allows. In الصيني (“china”, from Ṣīn) the final yāʾ is taken as the accusative object.

sentences.t: فَجِئْتُ إِلَيْهَا وَأَخْرَبْتُ مَعَهَا رُفُوفَ الْبَيْتِ بِكُلِّ مَا عَلَيْهَا وَدُرْتُ عَلَى السُّقُوفِ وَعَلَى كُلِّ مَحَلٍّ أُخْرِبُهُ وَمَا كَانَ فَى الْبَيْتِ مِنَ الصِّينِيِّ وَغَيْرِ ذَٰلِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-jiʾtu ilayhā wa-akhrabtu maʿahā rufūfa al-bayti bi-kulli mā ʿalayhā wa-durtu ʿalā al-suqūfi wa-ʿalā kulli maḥallin ukhribuhu wa-mā kāna fī al-bayti min al-ṣīniyyi wa-ghayri dhālika
sentences.l: And-I-came to-her and-ruined with-her the shelves-of the house with-all what [was] upon-them, and-went-round upon the ceilings, and-upon every place, I-ruin-it, and-what was in the house of the china and-other-than that…
sentences.i: So I went to her and wrecked the shelves of the house with her, with everything on them; I went round the ceilings and every spot, wrecking as I went, and all the china in the house and whatever else was there…
sentences.n: This sentence continues into the next. The print’s فى (with the dotless final letter) is kept; it is the ordinary في.

sentences.t: حَتَّى أَخْرَبْتُ الْجَمِيعَ وَأَنَا أَصِيحُ وَاسَيِّدَاهْ
sentences.tr: ḥattā akhrabtu al-jamīʿa wa-anā aṣīḥu wā-sayyidāh
sentences.l: …until I-had-ruined the whole, and-I cry: “O my-master!”
sentences.i: …until I had ruined it all, all the while crying, “Alas, my master!”
sentences.n: The cry واسيداه is the lament “wā sayyidāh”, “Oh, my lord!”, with the wā of lament.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ خَرَجَتْ سِتِّي مَكْشُوفَةَ الْوَجْهِ بِغِطَاءِ رَأْسِهَا لَاغَيْرَ
sentences.tr: thumma kharajat sittī makshūfata al-wajhi bi-ghiṭāʾi raʾsihā lā ghayra
sentences.l: Then went-out my-lady, uncovered-of the face, with-covering-of her-head, no other.
sentences.i: Then my lady came out with her face bare, wearing only her head-cloth and nothing more.

sentences.t: وَخَرَجَتْ مَعَهَا الْبَنَاتُ وَالأَوْلَادُ
sentences.tr: wa-kharajat maʿahā al-banātu wa-al-awlādu
sentences.l: And-went-out with-her the girls and-the children.
sentences.i: The daughters and the children came out with her.

sentences.t: وَقَالُوا يَا كَافُورُ امْشِ قُدَّا مَنَا وَأَرِنَا مَكَانَ سَيِّدِكَ الَّذِي هُوَ فِيهِ تَحْتَ الْحَائِطِ مَيِّتٌ
sentences.tr: wa-qālū yā kāfūru imshi quddā manā wa-arinā makāna sayyidika alladhī huwa fīhi taḥta al-ḥāʾiṭi mayyitun
sentences.l: And-they-said: O Kāfūr, walk in-front of-us and-show-us the-place-of your-master who he [is] in-it, under the wall, dead…
sentences.i: And they said, “Kāfūr, walk before us and show us the place where your master lies dead beneath the wall…
sentences.n: قدا منا is the print’s division of قدامنا, “before us”, pointed as two pieces. The clause continues into the next sentence.

sentences.t: حَتَّى نُخْرِجَهُ مِنْ تَحْتِ الرَّدْمِ وَنَحْمِلَهُ فِي تَابُوتٍ وَنَجِيً بِهِ إِلَى الْبَيْتِ فَنُخْرِجَهُ خُرْجَةً مَلِيحَةً
sentences.tr: ḥattā nukhrijahu min taḥti al-radmi wa-naḥmilahu fī tābūtin wa-najīʾa bihi ilā al-bayti fa-nukhrijahu khurjatan malīḥatan
sentences.l: …until we-bring-him-out from under the rubble, and-carry-him in a-coffin, and-bring with-him to the house, and-we-take-him-out a-going-out, a-fine-one.
sentences.i: …so that we may dig him out from under the rubble, carry him in a coffin, bring him home, and give him a proper funeral.”
sentences.n: The print marks the final yāʾ of ونجيً with a tanwīn sign, where نجيء (najīʾa, “that we bring”) is meant. I keep the mark in place. خرجة is a “going-out”, that is, a funeral procession.

sentences.t: فَمَشَيْتُ قُدَّامَهُمْ وَأَنَا أَصِيحُ وَا سَيِّدَاهْ
sentences.tr: fa-mashaytu quddāmahum wa-anā aṣīḥu wā sayyidāh
sentences.l: And-I-walked in-front-of-them, and-I cry: “O my-master!”
sentences.i: So I walked before them, crying, “Alas, my master!”

sentences.t: وَهُمْ خَلْفِي مَكْشُوفُونَ الْوُجُوهِ وَالرُّوُسِ يَصِيحُونَ أَوَّاهْ أَوَّاهْ عَلَى الرَّجُلِ
sentences.tr: wa-hum khalfī makshūfūna al-wujūhi wa-al-ruwusi yaṣīḥūna awwāh awwāh ʿalā al-rajuli
sentences.l: And-they behind-me, uncovered-ones of-the-faces and-the-heads, they-cry: “Alas! Alas!” over the man.
sentences.i: They came after me, faces and heads uncovered, crying “Alas! Alas!” for the man.
sentences.n: The print marks a damma on the waw of الروس (for الرؤوس, “the heads”); it is kept in place.

sentences.t: فَلَمْ يَبْقَ أَحَدٌ فَى الْحَارَةِ لَامِنَ الرِّجَالِ وَلَا مِنَ النِّسَاءِ وَلَامِنَ الصِّبْيَانِ وَلَا عَجُوزٌ إِلَّاجَاءَ مَعَنَا
sentences.tr: fa-lam yabqa aḥadun fī al-ḥārati lā min al-rijāli wa-lā min al-nisāʾi wa-lā min al-ṣibyāni wa-lā ʿajūzun illā jāʾa maʿanā
sentences.l: And-not remained anyone in the quarter, neither of the men nor of the women nor of the boys nor an-old-woman, except he-came with-us.
sentences.i: Not a soul was left in the quarter, neither man nor woman nor boy nor crone, but came along with us.
sentences.n: لامن and الاجاء are printed as single words (لا من, إلا جاء). The last two clauses are broken in the Arabic: after “nor of the boys” the construction changes to “nor an old woman”.

sentences.t: وَصَارُوا كُلُّهُمْ يَلْطِمُونَ مَعَنَا سَاعَةً وَهُمْ فِي شِدَّةِ الْبُكَاءِ
sentences.tr: wa-ṣārū kulluhum yalṭimūna maʿanā sāʿatan wa-hum fī shiddati al-bukāʾi
sentences.l: And-became all-of-them they-strike with-us an-hour, and-they in intensity-of the weeping.
sentences.i: And all of them beat their faces along with us for an hour, in the depth of their weeping.

sentences.t: فَشَقَّيْتُ لَهُمُ الْمَدِينَةَ
sentences.tr: fa-shaqqaytu lahumu al-madīnata
sentences.l: And-I-cleft for-them the city.
sentences.i: I led them through the city, cleaving a way for them.
sentences.n: The print has شقيت, which I read as the doubled شَقَّيْتُ, “I cut a way through”. The form is obscure; the sense of leading the mourners across town is clear.

sentences.t: فَسأَلَ النَّاسُ عَنِ الْخَبَرِ فَأَخْبَرُوهُمْ بِمَا سَمِعُوا مِنِّي
sentences.tr: fa-saʾala al-nāsu ʿani al-khabari fa-akhbarūhum bi-mā samiʿū minnī
sentences.l: And-asked the people about the news, and-they-informed-them with-what they-heard from-me.
sentences.i: The townsfolk asked what had happened, and the mourners told them what they had heard from me.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ النَّاسُ لَاحَوْلَ وَلَا قُوَّةَ إِلَّا بِاللَّهِ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla al-nāsu lā ḥawla wa-lā quwwata illā bi-allāhi
sentences.l: And-said the people: No power and-no strength except with-God.
sentences.i: And the people said, “There is no power and no strength but in God.”
sentences.n: لاحول is printed as one word.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ بَعْضُ النَّاسِ مَا هُوَ إِلَّارَجُلٌ كَبِيرٌ امْضِي لِلْوَالِي وَنُخْبِرُهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla baʿḍu al-nāsi mā huwa illā rajulun kabīrun imḍī li-al-wālī wa-nukhbiruhu
sentences.l: And-said some-of the people: He [is] not except a-man, a-great-one; go to-the-governor, and-we-inform-him.
sentences.i: Then some of them said, “He is a man of consequence. Let us go to the governor and tell him.”
sentences.n: الارجل is printed as one word (إلا رجل). The form امضي is written with a final yāʾ, as for a woman or as a plural “let us go”; it is pointed as the plain command “go on”, and the sense is that of “let us go to the governor and tell him”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا وَصَلُوا إِلَى الْوَالِي وَأَخْبَرُوهُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā waṣalū ilā al-wālī wa-akhbarūhu
sentences.l: And-when they-arrived at the governor and-informed-him…
sentences.i: And when they reached the governor and told him…
sentences.n: This sentence is cut short by the dawn; the sentence it begins is completed in the next night.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَزَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُب—احِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mub—āḥi
sentences.l: And-overtook Shahrazād the morning, and-she-fell-silent from the speech, the permitted.
sentences.i: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving her permitted speech.
sentences.n: The last word is damaged in the print as المب—اح, a dash standing in the place of a letter. It is read as المباح (al-mubāḥ, “the permitted”), the usual closing formula in which Shahrazād falls silent from permitted speech; the damaged form is kept exactly, with only its vowels added.
